questions.q: What is the mandatory structural element that distinguishes a formal report from an article in CBSE Class 11 English Core?
questions.a: A formal report requires a headline, byline (reporter's name/designation), and a lead paragraph answering the 5Ws (Who, What, When, Where, Why), while an article requires a headline, byline, and an introductory paragraph that hooks the reader but does not necessarily compress all 5Ws. A wrong answer (e.g., "both need a headline and byline only") reveals the student cannot differentiate format-specific skeletons, leading to hybrid pieces that lose format marks.

questions.q: Explain why embedding the phrase "The ritual resins had hardened, cementing Tut to the bottom of his solid gold coffin" as direct speech in a formal letter to the Director of the Egyptian Museum would be inappropriate.
questions.a: Formal letters require reported/indirect speech for textual evidence to maintain objective tone; direct quotes from the chapter disrupt the letter's professional register. A student who uses direct speech here confuses literary analysis conventions (where quoting is standard) with formal correspondence conventions (where paraphrasing with attribution is expected), indicating a misunderstanding of audience-purpose-format alignment.

questions.q: You are writing an analytical paragraph on "Science vs Tradition in Discovering Tut". Using PEEL structure, draft the Point and Evidence sentences only, citing two distinct textual details.
questions.a: Point: The chapter portrays a tension between modern scientific investigation and ancient funerary traditions. Evidence: The CT scan conducted in 2005 used "hundreds of X-rays in cross section" to create a "three-dimensional virtual body", while the ancient priests had sealed Tut with "ritual resins" meant to "guarantee resurrection" and the "pharaoh's curse" was still feared by tourists. A wrong answer that lists only one detail or merges them without contrast shows inability to select and juxtapose evidence for analytical depth.

questions.q: Compare the organizational logic of a newspaper report on Tut's CT scan with an article on "Ethics of Disturbing Ancient Remains". How does the paragraph sequencing differ?
questions.a: A report follows inverted pyramid: most critical facts (scan completion, findings, quotes from Hawass) in lead, then descending importance (technical details, historical background, curse anecdote). An article uses thematic sequencing: introduction framing the ethical debate, body paragraphs each exploring a dimension (scientific value, cultural respect, tourism impact), and a concluding synthesis. A student who sequences both identically fails to recognize that reports prioritize timeliness/facts while articles prioritize argument development.

questions.q: Evaluate this opening sentence for a formal letter to the Archaeological Survey of India: "I am writing to tell you that the CT scan of King Tut was awesome and we should do more such scans." Justify your evaluation with two specific flaws.
questions.a: The sentence is unacceptable: (1) Colloquial language ("awesome", "tell you") violates formal register; (2) Vague purpose ("we should do more such scans") lacks specific actionable request (e.g., "recommend a policy for non-invasive scanning of royal mummies"). A student who rates this as "good because it states the topic" reveals inability to distinguish academic/informal tone and to formulate precise official correspondence objectives.

questions.q: Create a headline, byline, and lead paragraph (30 words) for a report on the CT scan night, incorporating the scanner malfunction and the "Curse of the pharaoh" joke.
questions.a:
HEADLINE: CT Scan Reveals Tut's Secrets Despite Sandstorm Glitch
BYLINE: By [Name], Staff Correspondent
LEAD: Luxor, Jan 5: King Tutankhamun's mummy underwent a historic CT scan tonight, yielding 1,700 cross-sectional images despite a cooler-fan failure that prompted a guard's nervous "Curse of the pharaoh" quip. A weak answer that omits the byline, exceeds word limit, or buries the malfunction in later sentences shows poor grasp of report conciseness and news values.
